sources.entry: Memory Dependence Prediction using Store Sets - The origin of memory dependence prediction, which lets a load pass older stores and flushes on a wrong guess.

summary.title: Memory Dependence Prediction using Store Sets
summary.one_liner: Store sets track which earlier stores each load has conflicted with, letting out-of-order processors issue loads early while avoiding most memory-order violations and false dependencies.
keywords: how cpus handle load store ordering
takeaways: Conservative load scheduling avoids memory-order violations but creates many false dependencies that can slow some benchmarks by a factor of two or more.
A load's store set is the set of stores it has ever depended on, learned from past memory-order violations.
Store-set prediction makes loads wait only for stores in their set, approaching the performance of a perfect predictor in the paper's simulations.
Limiting a store set to one store or restricting a store to one set hurts performance; allowing multiple stores per load matters.
summary.summary: The paper motivates memory dependence prediction for wide out-of-order processors, where loads must issue early but must not read stale data from earlier stores. The authors compare no speculation and naive speculation against a perfect predictor using an eight-wide simulated Alpha-like CPU running SPEC95 benchmarks. They define store sets, built from observed memory-order violations, and evaluate idealized configurations for violations and false dependencies. The later sections propose a low-cost, direct-mapped implementation that is evaluated for near-optimal performance.
